passages.t: ‘Do not rebuke me in Your anger’: sickness, sin, and friends who stand far off
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of David, for remembrance” (verse 1). It begins with the same words as Psalm 6: “O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath” (verse 1).

He is very ill, and he connects his illness with his sin. “There is no soundness in my body because of Your anger; there is no rest in my bones because of my sin” (verse 3). “For my iniquities have overwhelmed me; they are a burden too heavy to bear” (verse 4). He describes his body in painful detail: wounds that fester, burning pain, a pounding heart, failing eyes (verses 5-10).

Worse than the pain is the loneliness. “My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance” (verse 11). Enemies plot against him, and he does not answer them: “like a mute man, I do not open my mouth” (verse 13).

He turns to God instead. “I wait for You, O LORD; You will answer, O Lord my God” (verse 15). “Yes, I confess my iniquity; I am troubled by my sin” (verse 18). The psalm ends without any answer yet, only a plea: “Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
This is a lament and one of the church's seven penitential psalms, prayers of sorrow for sin (see the note on Psalm 6). ‘For remembrance’ also heads Psalm 70. Its meaning is not certain. It may ask God to remember the one who prays.

In Israel, as in the whole ancient world, many people assumed that serious illness was a sign of God's anger. That is one reason friends kept away (verse 11). A long illness could also mean poverty, since a sick man could not work his land. There were doctors, but little medicine.

This man believes his own sin lies behind his suffering. He says so honestly. He does not blame anyone else, and he does not argue with God. He confesses.
passages.later:
Job, a righteous man, also felt that “the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me” (Job 6:4), and the whole book of Job argues that suffering is not always punishment. Jesus said the same. Asked whose sin had made a man blind, he answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). Of eighteen people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No” (Luke 13:4-5).

Jesus also knew the silence of verse 13. Before his accusers, like Isaiah's servant, “He did not open His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). And at his death, his friends “stood at a distance watching” (Luke 23:49), as the friends do in verse 11.
passages.hard:
Does this psalm mean that sickness is God's punishment for sin?

It means that this man, at this time, believed his illness was tied to his sin, and he brought both to God. It does not teach that every illness is a punishment. The rest of the Bible says plainly that it is not: the book of Job, and Jesus in John 9 and Luke 13. If you are ill, this psalm does not mean God is punishing you. Please do not let anyone tell you that it does.

Some readers will still feel, like this man, a weight of guilt alongside their pain. If that is you, the Psalms meet you. Psalm 32 tells what confession did for one guilty man, and Psalm 51 gives words to pray. Paul writes that “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

Illness also needs real care. James tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray for them (James 5:14), and seeing a doctor is wise; it is not a lack of faith. If your pain or guilt has become too heavy to bear alone, tell someone you trust. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
The psalm lets you be honest about pain and about sin at the same time, without pretending either is small.

It also asks something of the healthy. Verse 11 is a quiet rebuke to friends who keep their distance from the sick. Who do you know who is ill and alone? The psalm asks you not to stand far off.
